title: Control Who Builds On Your Platform Before You Open The Doors
documentTitle: Email from Neal Mohan to Jonathan Bellack et al. Re: PubMatic Ad Price Prediction (June 25, 2009)
excerptForBlog:
We should discuss this offline. I'm not comfortable opening up the XFP APIs to the YMs at this point.

— Neal Mohan

Jonathan Bellack had written: We are not including the Yield Managers in the trusted tester program, but once we take the API public in Q3/Q4 when the GAM pubs upgrade, we won't be able to pick and choose who gets access. We will have a terms of service and can look at what non-compete constraints we might want, but I think we should be as inclusive as possible to drive platform stickiness. Plus there are not any APIs into the ad selection process due to latency concerns, so the yield managers won't be able to do dynamic allocation. They try a workaround like updating the CPM of network line items dynamically but our initial API quotas will likely put a limit on how up-to-date they could keep things. I also expect that over time we'll institute API charges for 3rd-parties like what AdWords does, so this is actually a good revenue opportunity too.

Neal Mohan had earlier noted: Of all the 3rd party developer categories, yield managers are the ones I am most nervous about in terms of access to our new XFP API. It's fine if they participate via the AdX seller APIs.

lessonTitle: Control Who Builds On Your Platform Before You Open The Doors
pullQuote: Once you open a platform to everyone, you lose the right to choose who gets to compete with you on it — so pick your moment carefully.
situation: It's June 2009. Google is preparing to open a new API for its ad server (XFP) to outside developers. Jonathan Bellack argues for broad access — more partners means more platform stickiness, plus a future revenue stream from API fees. Neal Mohan pushes back twice, saying he is 'most nervous' about one specific category: yield managers (YMs) like PubMatic.
insight: Bellack is thinking about platform growth. Mohan is thinking about competitive positioning. The difference matters. Yield managers sit between publishers and ad exchanges — they optimize where ad inventory gets sold. If they get deep API access to XFP's ad selection logic, they can route around Google's own exchange (AdX) when it suits them. Mohan's carve-out — 'it's fine if they participate via the AdX seller APIs' — is the tell. He isn't blocking them entirely; he's channeling them through the part of the stack Google controls. This is classic platform strategy: open where it builds the network, closed where it protects the core. Bellack notes that 'latency concerns' already limit dynamic allocation through the API, but Mohan doesn't trust a technical speed bump as a long-term defense. He wants a structural one.
application: When you design API or partner access tiers, map each partner category to a simple question: does giving them this data or capability strengthen your position or someone else's? Grant access liberally where it drives adoption. Gate it specifically where a partner could use it to redirect value away from your core. One document cannot show how this decision ultimately played out, so treat this as a framing lens, not a proven playbook.
